title: NVDA vs AMD
asOf: Fundamentals: NVDA FY2026 (ended Jan 25, 2026), AMD FY2025 (ended Dec 27, 2025). Market data: Oct 6, 2026.
takeaways: The single biggest difference is profitability: NVDA keeps 71c of every sales dollar as gross profit and 56c as net profit, versus AMD's 50c and 13c — a 43-point net-margin gap driven by NVDA's pricing power.

The market prices both for growth, but in different ways: NVDA trades at ~49x trailing earnings while AMD trades at ~245x GAAP (~156x non-GAAP) — yet on price-to-sales AMD (30.3x) is valued slightly richer than NVDA (26.4x).
The risk the numbers surface is concentration: ~90% of NVDA's revenue rides on Compute & Networking (AI data center). AMD is balanced — 48% data center, 42% client & gaming, 10% embedded.

metrics.label: Market capitalization
metrics.reading: NVDA is valued at roughly 5.4x AMD — the market's scoreboard on their AI-data-center positions.

explain.what: The total market value of all outstanding shares: share price times shares outstanding.
explain.why: It is the market's collective verdict on what the entire company is worth, and it sets the scale of expectations — a $3T company is priced for a very different future than a $300B one.
explain.good: There is no 'good' absolute value; the useful read is relative. NVDA's market cap runs several multiples of AMD's, which reflects the market's view of their current AI-data-center positions.
explain.means: The gap reflects NVDA's dominant AI-accelerator share and 65% revenue growth. Market caps move daily; the ratio matters more than the level. Watch whether AMD's data-center growth narrows it.

metrics.label: Enterprise value

nvda.note: Market cap adjusted for net-cash position.

amd.note: Market cap adjusted for net-cash position.

metrics.reading: Nearly identical to market cap — both carry almost no net debt.

explain.what: Market capitalization plus total debt minus cash — roughly what an acquirer would pay for the whole company, free of obligations.
explain.why: It puts companies with different debt and cash levels on equal footing, which market cap alone cannot do.
explain.good: Judge it against revenue or operating profit rather than on its own; the ratio tells you more than the number.
explain.means: With both companies in a net-cash position, enterprise value adds little beyond market cap here. The comparison stays clean.

metrics.label: Revenue (TTM)
metrics.reading: NVDA's sales are 6.2x AMD's — different weight classes.

explain.what: Total sales over the trailing twelve months.
explain.why: The top line. Every margin, return, and valuation multiple flows from this number, so its size and trajectory anchor the whole comparison.
explain.good: For large semiconductor companies, sustained double-digit growth is strong. Both NVDA and AMD have recently grown revenue above 30% year over year.
explain.means: Scale compounds NVDA's R&D advantage: its $18.5B R&D budget alone exceeds half of AMD's total revenue. Watch AMD's Data Center growth rate — it is the line that could change the scale story.

explain.what: Reported headcount.
explain.why: Scale of the organization — and combined with revenue, it hints at business-model leverage. Chip designers run far leaner per revenue dollar than manufacturers.
explain.good: Revenue per employee above $1M marks an elite, highly leveraged model; both companies clear that bar by a wide margin.
explain.means: Headcount was not pulled for this mock. Revenue per employee will be added with SEC-sourced figures before user testing.

metrics.label: P/E ratio (trailing)

nvda.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release. NVDA: $239.24 / $4.90 FY2026 GAAP EPS. AMD: $649.42 / $2.65 GAAP; non-GAAP $4.17.

amd.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release. NVDA: $239.24 / $4.90 FY2026 GAAP EPS. AMD: $649.42 / $2.65 GAAP; non-GAAP $4.17.

metrics.reading: AMD's GAAP multiple is ~5x NVDA's — the market prices far more growth per current dollar of AMD earnings.

explain.what: Share price divided by earnings per share over the last twelve months.
explain.why: It states what you pay for each dollar of current earnings — the market's price tag on today's profitability.
explain.good: Semiconductor leaders often trade at 20–40x earnings during growth phases. Above 50x, the price assumes a great deal of future growth.
explain.means: The gap is mostly accounting: AMD's GAAP earnings are depressed by amortization from the Xilinx acquisition, so the non-GAAP 156x is the cleaner read — still over 3x NVDA's. It implies the market expects AMD's earnings to grow much faster from a smaller base. Watch whether AMD's GAAP and non-GAAP earnings converge.

explain.what: Share price divided by analysts' estimated earnings for the next twelve months.
explain.why: It shows what you pay for expected rather than past earnings, so it bakes in the market's growth assumptions.
explain.good: It usually sits below trailing P/E when earnings are expected to grow. Estimates are opinions, not facts — treat the ratio as a sentiment gauge.
explain.means: Analyst earnings estimates were not pulled for this mock. Forward multiples will be added with dated estimate sources.

metrics.label: Price / sales

nvda.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release.

amd.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release.

metrics.reading: The market pays slightly more per dollar of AMD's sales than NVDA's — despite NVDA's far higher margins.

explain.what: Share price divided by sales per share.
explain.why: Useful when earnings swing sharply, as they do in chip cycles — it values the revenue stream directly.
explain.good: Semiconductor companies often trade at 5–15x sales; above 20x, the market is pricing in exceptional, sustained growth.
explain.means: This is the most interesting valuation row: NVDA converts sales to profit far better, yet AMD's revenue fetches the higher multiple. It implies expectations of AMD gaining data-center share. Watch AMD's Data Center segment growth against NVDA's Compute & Networking.

explain.what: Enterprise value divided by earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization.
explain.why: It compares operating value while ignoring financing and accounting choices, making it the standard yardstick in acquisitions.
explain.good: A range of 15–25x is typical for quality semiconductor businesses.
explain.means: EBITDA requires depreciation detail not pulled for this mock. It will be added from 10-K cash-flow statements.

explain.what: The P/E ratio divided by the earnings growth rate.
explain.why: It adjusts the price tag for how fast earnings are growing — a high P/E matters less if earnings are doubling.
explain.good: Around 1.0 is the classic 'fair' marker. Well below 1 alongside real growth stands out; well above 1 means growth is fully priced.
explain.means: PEG needs a reliable forward EPS growth rate, which was not gathered for this mock.

metrics.label: Price / free cash flow

nvda.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release. NVDA FCF $96.6B (company-defined, Q4/FY2026 release). AMD FCF $5.5B (company-defined).

amd.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release. NVDA FCF $96.6B (company-defined, Q4/FY2026 release). AMD FCF $5.5B (company-defined).

metrics.reading: AMD's price is ~3x richer per dollar of free cash flow.

explain.what: Share price divided by free cash flow per share.
explain.why: It values the actual cash the business generates rather than accounting earnings.
explain.good: Profitable semiconductor companies often trade at 20–35x free cash flow.
explain.means: Cash is the hardest metric to argue with, and here the market's growth bet on AMD is starkest. For the multiple to normalize, AMD's free cash flow must grow several-fold from $5.5B. Watch quarterly FCF conversion.

metrics.label: Revenue growth (1Y)

nvda.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release.

amd.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release.

metrics.reading: Both growing fast; NVDA nearly twice as fast off a 6x larger base.

explain.what: The year-over-year change in sales.
explain.why: The simplest momentum read — it shows whether demand for the company's products is expanding right now.
explain.good: Above 20% is strong for a large semiconductor company; both NVDA and AMD have recently exceeded 30%.
explain.means: 65% growth on $216B of revenue is historically extraordinary — it added roughly $85B of new sales in one year, more than twice AMD's total revenue. Watch whether NVDA's growth decelerates as the base gets larger.

metrics.label: Revenue CAGR (5Y)

nvda.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release. NVDA covers FY2022-FY2026 (4Y); AMD covers 2021-2025 (5Y). Periods labeled, not mixed.

amd.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release. NVDA covers FY2022-FY2026 (4Y); AMD covers 2021-2025 (5Y). Periods labeled, not mixed.

metrics.reading: NVDA compounded at 68% — one of the fastest scalings in semiconductor history.

explain.what: The annualized growth rate of revenue over five years.
explain.why: It separates a one-year spike from a durable trend — sustained compounding is what builds long-term value.
explain.good: A 5-year CAGR above 15% is elite for a chip company; above 30% is historically rare.
explain.means: NVDA's trajectory reflects the AI buildout landing almost entirely on its products. AMD's 20% CAGR is itself strong — in line with the best large-cap chip compounders. The question for both is whether either rate survives the next cycle. (NVDA shown as 4Y: FY2022 is the earliest press-release-sourced year.)

explain.what: The year-over-year change in earnings per share.
explain.why: It shows whether profit is growing as fast as sales. EPS outpacing revenue means margins are expanding — operating leverage at work.
explain.good: EPS growth above revenue growth is the healthy pattern; the reverse warns that growth is coming at the cost of profitability.
explain.means: Year-over-year EPS growth was not computed for this mock; it will use split-adjusted diluted EPS from 10-Ks.

metrics.label: Gross margin

nvda.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release.

amd.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release.

metrics.reading: A 21-point gap — the clearest measure of NVDA's pricing power.

explain.what: The share of each sales dollar left after paying to make the product.
explain.why: It is the clearest read on pricing power. A company that charges far above its production cost usually has something competitors cannot easily copy — a technology lead or a position customers cannot switch out of cheaply.
explain.good: For semiconductor designers, 45–60% is typical; above 65% signals unusual pricing power.
explain.means: NVDA keeps 71¢ of each sales dollar versus AMD's 50¢. It suggests buyers currently have few substitutes for NVDA's AI accelerators. Watch whether the gap narrows as AMD's Instinct line and custom-silicon alternatives ship in volume.

metrics.label: Operating margin

nvda.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release.

amd.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release.

metrics.reading: A 50-point gap — NVDA's model scales; AMD's is still scaling.

explain.what: The share of sales left after operating costs such as R&D and sales.
explain.why: It shows whether the business model scales. R&D-heavy chip companies typically display operating leverage when the model works — profit growing faster than spending.
explain.good: A range of 25–40% is strong for semiconductor companies.
explain.means: NVDA converts revenue to operating profit at nearly 6x AMD's rate — extreme operating leverage. AMD's 11% is up from 2% in 2023, so the direction is right. Watch AMD's operating margin trend as data-center mix rises.

metrics.label: Net margin

nvda.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release.

amd.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release.

metrics.reading: The bottom-line gap: 43 points — the single widest in this comparison.

explain.what: The share of sales that becomes bottom-line profit.
explain.why: The final scorecard of the whole business after every cost, tax, and interest payment.
explain.good: Above 20% is strong; sustained margins above 50% are historically rare in any industry.
explain.means: More than half of NVDA's revenue becomes profit, a rarity in any industry. AMD's 12.5% is its best in years but shows how far the mix must shift. Watch AMD's data-center share of revenue — it carries the highest margins.

explain.what: Operating profitability before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization, as a share of sales.
explain.why: It gives a cleaner peer comparison by removing financing and accounting choices.
explain.good: A range of 30–50% is typical for leading semiconductor companies.
explain.means: EBITDA margin was not computed for this mock; it will be added with depreciation detail from 10-Ks.

metrics.label: Return on equity (ROE)

nvda.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release. NVDA: $120.1B net income / $157.3B equity. AMD: $4.3B / $63.0B.

amd.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release. NVDA: $120.1B net income / $157.3B equity. AMD: $4.3B / $63.0B.

metrics.reading: NVDA earns an extraordinary return on equity; AMD's is modest but recovering.

explain.what: Net income divided by shareholder equity — the return on the owners' money.
explain.why: It measures how well management compounds the capital entrusted to it.
explain.good: Above 15% is solid and above 30% is exceptional. Note that heavy share repurchases shrink equity and can flatter this ratio.
explain.means: 76% ROE means NVDA's annual profit is three-quarters of its entire equity base — though share repurchases flatter it by shrinking equity. AMD's 6.9% reflects the Xilinx-inflated equity base. Watch AMD's ROE as acquisition amortization fades.

metrics.label: Return on assets (ROA)

nvda.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release.

amd.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release.

metrics.reading: NVDA's asset base is extraordinarily productive; AMD's is weighed by acquisition goodwill.

explain.what: Net income divided by total assets.
explain.why: It shows how efficiently the asset base generates profit. Asset-light chip designers naturally score higher than manufacturers.
explain.good: Above 10% is good for a semiconductor company.
explain.means: AMD carries ~$25B of goodwill from Xilinx, which depresses ROA without affecting cash generation — the ratio understates its operating reality. Watch tangible-asset returns for the cleaner read.

explain.what: After-tax operating profit divided by invested capital (equity plus interest-bearing debt).
explain.why: The purest value-creation test: when ROIC exceeds the cost of capital, growth creates value; below it, growth destroys value.
explain.good: Sustained ROIC above 15% marks a strong compounder.
explain.means: ROIC needs the effective tax rate to compute after-tax operating profit; it was not pulled for this mock.

metrics.label: Net debt

nvda.note: Negative = net cash position. Net debt = total debt minus cash & cash equivalents (excludes marketable securities / short-term investments).

amd.note: Negative = net cash position. Net debt = total debt minus cash & cash equivalents (excludes marketable securities / short-term investments).

metrics.reading: Both are net cash — neither needs creditors.

explain.what: Total debt minus cash and equivalents. A negative number means net cash.
explain.why: It answers whether the company could survive a bad year without raising money.
explain.good: Net cash (a negative number) is fortress-like. Both NVDA and AMD carry modest debt relative to their cash generation.
explain.means: Neither company has a balance-sheet constraint on R&D or share repurchases. NVDA additionally holds ~$52B in marketable securities beyond cash. This row is a clean bill of health for both — nothing to watch here.

metrics.label: Debt / equity

nvda.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release.

amd.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release.

metrics.reading: Identical and negligible — leverage is a non-issue for both.

explain.what: Total debt divided by shareholder equity.
explain.why: A leverage gauge — a high ratio means creditors carry more of the company's risk.
explain.good: Below 0.5 is comfortable for a semiconductor company.
explain.means: Both fund themselves overwhelmingly with equity. In a downturn, neither faces refinancing pressure.

explain.what: Current assets divided by current liabilities.
explain.why: It tests whether the company can cover the bills coming due within a year.
explain.good: Above 1.5 is healthy; above 2 is strong.
explain.means: Current assets and liabilities were not pulled for this mock; the ratio will be added from 10-K balance sheets.

metrics.label: Cash & equivalents

nvda.note: Includes marketable securities / short-term investments as stated.

amd.note: Includes marketable securities / short-term investments as stated.

metrics.reading: NVDA's liquid resources are ~6x AMD's.

explain.what: Cash on hand plus short-term liquid investments.
explain.why: Dry powder for R&D, share repurchases, acquisitions, and downturns — strategic flexibility in a cyclical industry.
explain.good: More is safer; the right context is revenue scale, not the absolute number.
explain.means: NVDA's $62.6B total liquidity funds years of R&D at the current pace alongside its $150B share repurchases authorization. AMD's $10.5B is ample for its scale. Watch cash conversion, not the stockpile.

metrics.label: Operating cash flow

nvda.note: AMD: continuing operations.

amd.note: AMD: continuing operations.

metrics.reading: NVDA generated nearly 16x AMD's operating cash.

explain.what: Cash generated from core business operations.
explain.why: It shows what the business actually collected in cash. Over time it usually tracks or exceeds net income; persistent divergence deserves a question, not an assumption.
explain.good: A healthy pattern is operating cash flow at or above net income across full cycles — cash backing the reported profit.
explain.means: Cash confirms the profit story — NVDA's earnings are real, collected dollars. AMD's $6.5B is a record and covers its needs several times over.

metrics.label: Free cash flow

nvda.source: NVIDIA Q4/FY2026 earnings press release, Feb 25, 2026
nvda.note: Company-defined free cash flow as reported by each company.

amd.note: Company-defined free cash flow as reported by each company.

metrics.reading: A ~$91B gulf in truly available cash.

explain.what: Operating cash flow minus capital spending — the cash truly available after keeping the business running.
explain.why: It funds share repurchases, dividends, and acquisitions. For investors, it is the most tangible output of the business.
explain.good: Positive and growing is the baseline; the margin below says how efficient the conversion is.
explain.means: After keeping the business running, NVDA has $96.6B to deploy — share repurchases, R&D, or strategic moves. AMD's $5.5B is its own record. Watch how each allocates it: NVDA's $150B share repurchases authorization against AMD's reinvestment needs.

metrics.label: FCF margin

nvda.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release. NVDA: $96.6B / $215.9B = 44.7%. AMD: $5.5B / $34.6B = 15.9%.

amd.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release. NVDA: $96.6B / $215.9B = 44.7%. AMD: $5.5B / $34.6B = 15.9%.

metrics.reading: NVDA converts 45¢ of each sales dollar to free cash; AMD converts 16¢.

explain.what: Free cash flow as a share of revenue.
explain.why: It shows how much of each sales dollar becomes usable cash.
explain.good: A range of 20–30% or higher is strong for semiconductor companies.
explain.means: The fabless model at its extreme: NVDA spends just 2.8% of revenue on capex, so nearly half of sales becomes cash. AMD matches the capex discipline at 2.8% but lower margins compress conversion. Watch AMD's FCF margin as data-center mix grows.

metrics.label: Capex intensity

nvda.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release.

amd.note: Computed from reported statement lines in our own arithmetic; inputs verified against the cited filing/release.

metrics.reading: Identical — the fabless model's signature.

explain.what: Capital spending as a share of revenue.
explain.why: Chip designers outsource manufacturing to foundries, so low capex intensity is the structural advantage of the fabless model.
explain.good: Below 5% is typical for fabless designers; far below the 20–30% that manufacturers must spend.
explain.means: Both outsource manufacturing to foundries such as TSMC, so neither must pour revenue into fabs. This is the structural reason their cash conversion can stay high through cycles.

explain.what: Share price change plus dividends over the last year.
explain.why: How owning the stock actually felt — the lived experience behind the fundamentals.
explain.good: Judge it against the semiconductor index, not in isolation; a 40% gain means little if the sector gained 60%.
explain.means: Twelve-month price history was not pulled for this mock; it will be added with a dated price series.

metrics.label: Beta

nvda.note: Point-in-time market data; sources differ slightly.

amd.note: Point-in-time market data; sources differ slightly.

metrics.reading: Both swing more than twice as hard as the market.

explain.what: How much the stock tends to move relative to the overall market (1.0 moves with the market).
explain.why: A volatility gauge — it describes the ride, not the destination.
explain.good: There is no 'good' value. Above 1 means bigger swings in both directions; both NVDA and AMD run above 1.

amd.note: Point-in-time market data; sources differ slightly.

explain.why: A quick sentiment snapshot — near the highs suggests momentum, near the lows suggests skepticism.
explain.good: The position alone does not say which interpretation is right; it frames the question the fundamentals must answer.
